sections.html:
The Columbia metro area includes Lexington County, in the Midlands, where Lake Murray accounts for much of the water. Lexington, the seat and largest community, had 23,568 residents in 2020. Countywide, people numbered 262,391 in 2010 and 293,991 in 2020, with 317,588 estimated for 2025.

New building clusters on the eastern and northeastern side, closest to Columbia. A lake-area house, a subdivision near Irmo and a rural parcel near Gilbert share a county but move on different timelines. Rapid growth usually lifts assessed values at the next reassessment, so someone who bought a few years back may find the bill larger than they budgeted. For a house near Lake Murray or the Saluda, Broad and Congaree rivers, look into drainage and flood questions yourself before a buyer's inspector raises them.

Collection, valuation and exemptions are split three ways: Treasurer, Assessor and Auditor.

OfficeContactWhat it handles
Treasurer212 South Lake Drive, Suite 101, Lexington, SC 29072; (803) 785-8217; Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.Payments, penalty appeals
Delinquent Tax Department(803) 785-8345Past-due accounts
Tax Assessor(803) 785-8190Exemptions, sales, address changes, appraisals, rollback taxes
Auditor(803) 785-8181Homestead exemptions, refunds

You can pay at the counter, on the web at lex-co.sc.gov, by check to PO Box 604397, Charlotte, NC 28260-4397, or at the night deposit box outside the County Administration Building. Card payments add convenience fees.

Notices for real property go out after October 1 to the owner of record. Pay the whole bill by the next January 15. A payment with a later postmark gathers penalties on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

Those penalties are 3 percent, 7 percent more and 5 percent more, per S.C. Code 12-45-180. Penalties continue to build during a penalty appeal unless you pay in full, and the county gives back what you paid if the appeal is granted. Send penalty appeals to the Treasurer in writing, and call (803) 785-8217 for instructions.

Mail only checks, and send them early, since the postmark is what counts. If the mail feels risky near the deadline, use the night deposit box or the online payment page instead.

Real property that is not paid through escrow is eligible for the county's installment program. Participants pay five advance installments set from the prior year's tax, and November 15 is when the leftover balance is billed.

You re-enroll yearly, and dropping out takes written consent. If you are enrolled and plan to sell, ask the Treasurer before closing how the plan will be handled. A forgotten enrollment is a frequent loose end after a house changes hands.

Your written appeal reaches the Assessor within 90 days of the notice date. Without a notice, the county's FAQ points to a January 1 through January 15 window the next year.

Market value is what an appeal tests. Calling the tax bill too large is not a valid ground. An appeal still pending on December 31 means billing at no less than 80 percent of assessed value, and payment is still owed January 15. After the ruling, interest applies either way: a refund to you or a balance owed.

A Board of Assessment Appeals with nine members, chosen by County Council, hears cases when asked, in the Council Chambers of the County Administration Building, and agendas appear on the county meeting portal. State rules entitle owners to notice of a rise of $1,000 or more. The county reappraised in 2015 and 2020, a five-year rhythm, and the Assessor can tell you the next date.

sections.h2: What changes when a house sells
sections.html:
Whatever the seller still owes for the year comes out of the proceeds at closing. The buyer files a separate application for the 4 percent legal residence ratio, due before the first penalty date of the year it is first claimed.

These are the loose ends that most often trip up Lexington County sellers:

  • A rental over the 72-day limit that was taxed at 6 percent.
  • An installment plan left active after the sale.
  • A bill that went to a former address because the Assessor was never told about the move.
  • A lake or older-neighborhood house that needs roof, septic or foundation work before a lender will finance the buyer.

If back tax and repairs both block a sale, selling as-is for cash lets the title company pay the county out of your proceeds. For the payoff and the tax sale schedule, call the Delinquent Tax Department at (803) 785-8345.

A short routine keeps the sale on track.

  1. See the Treasurer first: is the account paid, or in the installment plan? Get written instructions for leaving the plan if you are in it.
  2. Call the Auditor to find out whether a homestead exemption is on the account, and report the pending sale.
  3. Have the Assessor fix your mailing address and tell you whether rental use put the legal residence ratio at risk.
  4. If any bill has gone past due, ask the Delinquent Tax Department for a payoff.

Carry the deed or parcel number, your latest bill and a photo ID. Because the penalty dates are January 16, February 2 and March 17, an early quote goes stale, so request a new number once you have a closing date.

With a cash buyer there is no loan appraisal to wait for. Title work and the payoff set the pace instead, and you can start both the day you decide to sell.

sections.h2: Legal residence ratio and rental use
sections.html:
A house you live in is taxed on a 4 percent ratio, while other property is taxed on 6 percent. The 72-day rental limit is the line to watch: a home rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year loses the lower ratio. If you rented the house out at any point before selling, ask the Assessor how that affects the account.

The same ratio matters to your buyer. Someone who closes late in the year and does not file before the first penalty date pays at 6 percent for that year, so a note to your buyer about the deadline helps them as much as it helps you.

Three questions are worth settling before you sign. First, how much is still owed, and through what date does that figure hold? Second, has the Auditor heard about the sale, so the homestead exemption can come off? Third, does the Assessor have the buyer's mailing address for next year's notice? Your title company covers the first, and the other two are on you.

When a bill is already past due, the Delinquent Tax Department is the office to call. It can give you the amount and tell you where the account stands in the process.

faqs.q: When is Lexington County property tax due?
faqs.a: The whole amount is owed by January 15 of the year following the tax year, and penalties start on January 16.

faqs.q: Where is the Lexington County Treasurer's office?
faqs.a: 212 South Lake Drive, Suite 101, Lexington, SC 29072. The phone is (803) 785-8217, and hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Lexington County assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days from the date on the notice. If none came, the county's guidance is to appeal between January 1 and January 15 of the next year.

faqs.q: Does Lexington County have an installment plan?
faqs.a: Yes, if the property is not paid through escrow. Five advance payments are based on last year's tax, with the remainder billed by November 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lexington County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, and closing takes care of it, since the title company pays the balance from your proceeds. The Delinquent Tax Department, (803) 785-8345, can quote the current amount.
